children: By Karol Badohal, Gergely Szakacs and Libby George
Poland's surging debt earned it a credit rating downgrade last week - a red flag to investors concerned that it has little appetite to rein in spending ahead of a national election next year.
The central European economic powerhouse has been sustained by booming growth - but could find that a pre-election splurge saddles it with higher borrowing costs in the coming years.
The election is likely to be closely contested, with some of Prime Minister Donald Tusk's coalition allies struggling in the polls, the right-wing PiS shedding support and the far-right on the rise.

Moody's cut Poland's credit rating to A3 on Friday, citing large budget deficits, weakening debt affordability and a "limited willingness or ability" to shore up public finances despite buoyant growth.

Poland's roughly 60% debt-to-GDP ratio is well below an 87% euro zone average, according to Eurostat, but fiscal slippage, mirroring post-election budget blowouts in Hungary and Romania, is a growing worry.
"They are running an unsustainably high budget deficit and showing zero appetite to reduce it," said Viktor Szabo, a portfolio manager with Aberdeen.
POLISH 10-YEAR YIELDS UP 100 BASIS POINTS THIS YEAR
On Monday, Poland's local and foreign currency bonds moved sideways as markets largely anticipated the downgrade.
But 10-year Polish bond yields have increased by some 100 basis points this year, scaling 3-1/2-year highs, as a loose fiscal stance has compounded the impacts of a global bond market sell-off.
The International Monetary Fund expects Poland's strong growth to slow in the coming years.

Erste Group economists said that if global bond turmoil and regional security worries relating to Russia escalated, "the deterioration in Poland's rating could become a catalyst for a broader sell-off in the local financial market."

Malgorzata Krzywicka, director at Fitch Ratings, said "large deficits, rapidly rising public debt/GDP, and the absence of a credible fiscal consolidation strategy" were all challenges to Poland's rating.
The 2027 draft budget, which targets an unchanged deficit of 7.1%, “highlights the difficult fiscal position and risks ahead of next year's parliamentary elections", she added.
The IMF is projecting Poland's debt-to-GDP at 77.7% by 2031.
'FEELING WELL DOES NOT NEGATE BAD TEST RESULTS'
No major party has unveiled how it would rein in borrowing. Sławomir Dudek, head of the Fiscal Council watchdog, said Poland was acting like a patient with high cholesterol.
"Feeling well does not negate bad test results," he said on X. "Simply promising yourself 'I'll get my act together next year' won't improve your numbers."
Societe Generale economist Juan Orts said the winner of next year's election will have little time for complacency:
"If the future new government does not present a clear fiscal consolidation plan for 2028, the risk of downgrades will be materially higher."
